rv.q: A quietly devastating, gently funny and beautifully delivered piece of theatre, it shows us what it means to be one of those statistics.
Alexander Zeldin’s new play is not like anything I have seen before.
In the end, this is that rare thing: a necessary play that suggests Zeldin has taken on the role of the Victorian Henry Mayhew in compassionately documenting the lives of the urban poor.
The play eloquently distils the galling outrage of a political situation in which, as a society, the most we choose to offer to a starving family is a soggy cheese sandwich.

This new piece takes a similar perspective, considering the effects of poverty, marginalisation and our broken social-care system through a chorus of human stories that take care to show, rather than tell; to persuade, rather than preach.
Mostly this deeply loving, oddly riveting depiction of people hanging on quietly, but determinedly at the edge of despair lets us come to our own conclusions.
They radiate warmth, care and belief in people.
He still finds the hope in desperate circumstances, and can still catch you off-guard with a single line...
More often this is a heartbreaking portrayal of how the most vulnerable try to help one another.
Faith, Hope And Charity is touching, ferociously well played …..and incredibly slow.
Nevertheless, Faith, Hope and Charity seems to me an utterly necessary and deeply compassionate depiction of the kinds of lives that it is all too easy to ignore.
This is a painful, profound portrait of people in despair that is worth investing in.

There’s no doubting that Faith, Hope & Charity is necessary theatre, its honesty unflinching, its compassion complete – rather that, for its message to travel as widely as it should, it doesn’t quite hold together.

The skilful naturalism of the show conceals the socioeconomic reality: a middle-class audience has hired a troupe of actors (who are also middle class) to pose as impoverished dropouts for a night of escapist amusement.
There are well-meaning contributions from the cast and creatives, but nothing can solve the short-comings of a verbose, static, lifeless script.
Zeldin's work offers neither a solution nor an indictment.

cn.t: Zeldin's devastating trilogy closer about austerity-era Britain divides critics: most praise its quietly furious naturalism and Cecilia Noble's performance, though some find its slow pace and bleakness hard to endure.
